name: Carmen Cumberland
title: President & CEO
fit: Twenty-five years as CHFB's fiscal signatory plus four years Navy service have wired her to demand command relationships, sustainment, and decision points before she'll approve anything — a proposal without auditability is, to her, a plan without logistics. She reads every initiative the way an operational commander reads an operations order: intent, resourcing, risk, and a named point where the org decides to adjust or hold.
posture: She scores the organization the way she signs off on a Single Audit — conservatively, crediting only what she can point to evidence for, not aspiration. Where the scale is a tradeoff rather than a ladder, she answers from temperament: deliberate, mission-anchored, protective of scarce reserves, not chasing tempo for its own sake.

DS1.option: We periodically step back, not systematically
DS1.why: Volunteer floor and 300 agencies limit real sensing infrastructure

DC1.option: Mission is a consistent filter on decisions
DC1.why: I'm the last signature — mission has to hold

AS3.option: A few individuals experimenting, no org strategy
AS3.why: No slack in a 59-FTE shop for AI pilots yet

AC1.option: Slow, repetitive review cycles, months to approve
AC1.why: Auditability requirement is a real gate, not theater

XT1.option: Thorough before committing; deliberate over quick
XT1.why: Logistics discipline means I check supply lines first

TX1.why: New ideas get vetted against the mission first

DS2.option: Consistent practice of asking "why" multiple times
DS2.why: Auditor training — symptom fixes don't survive my review

DS3.option: Mix of incremental fixes and occasional rethink
DS3.why: We improve the wagon route before we reinvent it

DS4.option: Engaged — feedback gathered and folded into planning
DS4.why: Client-choice pantry model listens, but isn't co-design

DC2.option: Would trigger genuine reconsideration of the initiative
DC2.why: Values concerns get real airtime, not a courtesy nod

DC3.option: Intend to serve all, financial pressure dominates
DC3.why: Restricted funding and thin margins force hard tradeoffs

DC4.option: Occasionally, when leadership sees clear misalignment
DC4.why: We course-correct when the gap is obvious, not before

AS1.option: Monitor trends via FIsH, Feeding America network
AS1.why: Peer network is my early-warning picket line

AS2.option: Occasionally step back to question current methods
AS2.why: Single Audit cycle forces a look, not a habit

AS4.option: Frontline can share, but no clear channel up
AS4.why: Volunteers rotate too fast to build a reporting line

AC2.option: A quarter, with executive intervention and disruption
AC2.why: Restricted grants mean reallocation isn't a light switch

AC3.option: Delegated some, but default is seeking my approval
AC3.why: I'm the final institutional signatory — that's by design

AC4.option: Compliance functions gate adoption for safety, gradually
AC4.why: Auditability and compliance come before speed, full stop

DT1.option: Execution rhythm with intentional reflection built in
DT1.why: Rehearse, execute, assess — that's just operating tempo

DT2.option: Identify pain points, see if tech solves them
DT2.why: Prove the ROI on the problem we already have

AT1.option: Discuss thoroughly, struggle to move resources fast
AT1.why: Reserves are thin — I don't commit them lightly

AT2.option: Analyze the shift, understand why before reacting
AT2.why: I want the estimate of the situation first

TS1.why: We know our lane; changing it takes planning

TS2.option: Quickly investigate why, fix the implementation
TS2.why: Root-cause it, then execute the correction cleanly

TC1.option: Protecting and optimizing what's already working wins
TC1.why: Proven cost recovery beats an unproven bright idea

TC2.option: Protective of investments unless clearly underperforming long-term
TC2.why: We don't retire a program on a bad quarter

name: Katie Savoie
title: Director of Development
fit: Katie runs institutional fundraising, corporate sponsorships, and grant pipelines the way a BD director runs a channel portfolio — she diagnoses funder incentives before pitching and treats every foundation, retailer, and council relationship as an asset exchange, not a favor. She is also the person who translates an internal capacity gap into a grant-fundable ask, which makes her the org's de facto negotiator with its own risk-averse budget.
posture: She scores stakeholder-facing sensing and mission-alignment items high because reading donor and partner motive is her whole job; she scores internal agility and reallocation items low because she watches good ideas die in the org's own approval queue while corporate partners wait on an answer. On the tradeoff items she answers from temperament — action-biased and opportunity-chasing, tempered by a fundraiser's need to keep mission and donor trust intact.

DS1.why: Discovery on donor motive is literally my job

DC1.option: Meaningful input, but backseat to financial pressure sometimes

AS3.option: A few individuals experimenting, no org strategy yet
AS3.why: I'm the workaround, not the organizational muscle

AC1.option: Slow repetitive review cycles, approvals take months
AC1.why: Sponsors move faster than our own approval chain

XT1.option: Lean toward action, build in reflection as we go
XT1.why: Campaigns don't wait for a perfect plan

TX1.option: Lead with mission and strategy, filter new opportunities through it

DC2.why: I'd walk from a sponsor that costs us trust

name: Dearllean Walker
title: Warehouse Operations Manager
fit: Dearllean runs the floor like a service line — a rotating volunteer brigade that has to hit the same standard every single day with zero shared history and one minute of training. She thinks in stations, prep, and the gap between a demo that worked once and a line that survives real volume.
posture: She's blunt about how far the floor sits from strategy conversations — she scores those items low and unapologetically, because that's the honest read from where she stands. On anything about process discipline, consistency, and whether frontline reality reaches decision-makers, she answers with the specificity of someone who runs the actual pass every day.

DS1.option: Periodically step back on stakeholder needs, not systematic
DS1.why: We notice things change, but nobody's tracking it upstairs

DC1.option: Mission is general guidance, referenced when convenient
DC1.why: Mission talk doesn't touch what I decide on the floor

AS3.option: A few individuals experimenting, no org strategy
AS3.why: Somebody's playing with an app; nobody told the floor

AC1.option: Slow repetitive review cycles, months to approve
AC1.why: A new scanner takes forever to get approved here

XT1.option: Thorough before committing, deliberate over quick
XT1.why: I'd rather test it twice before it hits my line

TX1.option: Strong mission and strategy filters new opportunities
TX1.why: Leadership picks direction; I just execute it clean

DS2.option: Consistent practice of asking why to find root cause
DS2.why: If a pallet's wrong twice, I trace it back

DS3.option: Mix of incremental fixes and occasional rethink
DS3.why: Mostly I tighten the line, sometimes I redesign the station

DS4.option: Responsive — we listen to complaints and requests
DS4.why: Agencies call when something's off; that's the loop

DC2.option: Heard respectfully but probably wouldn't change the decision
DC2.why: Values get a nod, budget still wins upstairs

DC3.option: Intend to serve all, but financial pressure dominates
DC3.why: Money's tight, so tradeoffs usually go one way

DC4.option: Reluctantly reassess, only when forced by crisis
DC4.why: We don't touch a process till it breaks

AS1.option: Notices eventually, struggles to evaluate what it means
AS1.why: New tech shows up on my desk with no context

AS2.option: If it isn't broken, we don't revisit it
AS2.why: My line runs the same way it did last year

AC2.option: Six months to a year with real negotiation
AC2.why: Shifting staff or budget here takes forever

AC3.option: Some delegation, but people default to seeking approval

AC4.option: IT/compliance function as gatekeepers, adopt slowly and safely

AT1.option: Discuss thoroughly, struggle to move resources quickly
AT1.why: We talk it through, but moving fast isn't us

AT2.why: I watch how it plays out before I touch my line

TS1.option: Clear direction, needs real planning effort to adapt
TS1.why: We know our lane; changing it takes real work

TS2.option: Quickly investigate why to fix the implementation

TC1.option: Protecting and optimizing what's already working wins
